title: What smart people say about Nasdaq correction, down 10% from highs
excerpt: The Nasdaq 100 closed below 28,000 points on Monday, down 10.4% from its October 6 high. Market gurus pointed to AI worries and midterm jitters.
content_html:
What smart people are saying after the Nasdaq sank into correction territory

By Theron Mohamed

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

Is the AI-fueled market boom stalling out?

That was the question on investors' minds after the Nasdaq 100 slumped into a technical correction on Monday, defined as a decline of 10% or more from a recent peak.

The tech-heavy US stock index closed at just under 28,000 points, a hefty 10.4% below the all-time high of over 31,000 points it notched on October 6.

It was the Nasdaq 100's third correction of 2026, and came as investors increasingly asked when the massive sums that Big Tech is pouring into AI might pay off.

The Nasdaq 100 rallied out of correction territory in morning trading on Tuesday. It was up 0.7% at around 28,200 points as of 9:04 a.m. ET, leaving it down 9.7% from its previous high.

Here's what smart people are saying about the correction.

David Rosenberg, president of Rosenberg Research

A correction was "probably inevitable" given the huge volume of capital pouring into "any company claiming to have an AI angle," David Rosenberg, the president of Rosenberg Research, said in a morning note on Tuesday.

The former chief North American economist at Merrill Lynch said that "both sides of the AI trade are faltering at once." The likes of Microsoft and Alphabet have sold off because they're spending too much and eroding their cash flows, he continued, while their suppliers have sold off because "spending isn't speeding up."

"The overriding theme is that investors stopped rewarding the AI buildout and started asking when it pays back," Rosenberg added.

Jim Reid, head of macro research at Deutsche Bank

There isn't an "overt catalyst" for the Nasdaq correction, but "emerging expectations of a blue wave in the midterms" appear to be weighing on tech stocks, Jim Reid, the global head of macro research at Deutsche Bank, and his team said in a morning note.

Investors are pricing in the prospect of a Democratic victory resulting in "greater hurdles for data center buildout and a push for more AI regulation," Reid and his team added.

Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo UK

Fund managers are "just reducing overall exposure" to the AI trade as it's turned "ugly," Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo UK, told Business Insider by email on Tuesday.

Wilson pointed to Morgan Stanley data through late October showing that equity long/short hedge funds experienced their biggest gross-flow drawdown since the investment bank started tracking them in 2016.

He said there's "definitely a lot more scrutiny" on returns from AI investments, flagging that some recent hyperscaler earnings showed negative cash flows due to heavy spending on AI equipment.

"Bit of a bubble bursting moment," Wilson said.

The Kobeissi Letter

The correction in tech stocks reflects not just concerns about AI spending hurting profits, but investors "pricing in two years of political gridlock," The Kobeissi Letter, an industry commentary, said in an X post on Monday.

The newsletter's writers pointed to surging expectations of a Democrat sweep in the midterms, and President Trump vowing to be "Mr. Veto" if Republicans cede control of the House and Senate.
